title: What to Do After a Car Accident in Las Vegas: A Body Shop's Checklist
excerpt: A simple, step-by-step checklist for the first hours and days after a Las Vegas car accident, from the scene to getting your car repaired right.
seoTitle: What to Do After a Car Accident in Las Vegas | Checklist
metaDescription: Just had a car accident in Las Vegas? Follow this body shop checklist covering safety, photos, insurance, towing, and choosing a collision repair shop.

children.text: Nobody plans for a car accident. One minute you're driving down Decatur, the next you're standing on the shoulder trying to figure out what to do first. The first few hours after a crash can shape how smoothly the rest of the process goes, from your insurance claim to the quality of your repair.
Here's the checklist we walk our own customers through.
1. Make sure everyone is safe

Before anything else, check on yourself, your passengers, and the people in the other vehicle. If anyone is hurt, call 911 right away. If the cars can be moved and it's safe to do so, get them out of traffic and turn on your hazard lights.
2. Call the police when needed

For many accidents, especially ones involving injuries or significant damage, a police report is important. It gives your insurance company an official record of what happened. Even for smaller fender benders, it's worth knowing your options for filing a report so you have documentation later.
3. Document everything
Your phone is your best tool here. Take photos of:
All sides of every vehicle involved, close up and from a distance
License plates
The road, traffic signs, and any skid marks
Any visible injuries
Also exchange names, phone numbers, insurance information, and driver's license details with the other driver. If there are witnesses, ask for their contact info too.
4. Don't skip the hidden damage check

Modern vehicles are built to absorb impact, which means a bumper cover can look almost fine while the brackets, sensors, and crash structure behind it are damaged. Damage you can't see can affect how your car handles and how well it protects you in a future accident. That's why a full inspection matters, even when the damage looks minor.
5. Report the claim to your insurance company
Call your insurer as soon as you can and give them the facts. Stick to what you know, and share your photos and the police report number if you have one.
6. Get your car towed to the shop you trust

If your car isn't safe to drive, you'll need a tow. You don't have to let the car go wherever the tow truck or insurance company suggests. In Nevada, you can choose the licensed body shop that repairs your vehicle. At The Rebels Garage, we offer free towing with repairs, so getting your car to us is one less thing to worry about.
7. Get a detailed estimate
A good estimate should explain what's being repaired or replaced and why. If you have questions, ask them. A trustworthy shop will walk you through it, show you the damage, and explain your options.
The bottom line
The hours after an accident are stressful, but you don't have to figure it out alone. If you've been in an accident in Las Vegas, our
collision repair team
can inspect your vehicle, write up a free estimate, and work with your insurance company to get you back on the road.

title: Can You Choose Your Own Body Shop in Nevada? What Drivers Should Know
excerpt: After an accident, your insurance company may suggest a shop. Here's what Nevada law says about your right to choose where your car gets repaired.
seoTitle: Can You Choose Your Own Body Shop in Nevada?
metaDescription: Nevada drivers have the right to choose a licensed body shop after an accident. Learn what that means for your insurance claim and your repair.

children.text: After an accident, one of the first things many drivers hear from their insurance company is a recommendation for a body shop. Sometimes it's framed as the easiest option, or the only option. A lot of people don't realize they have a choice.
What Nevada law says

Under Nevada law (NRS 690B.016), a policyholder or claimant can have their vehicle repaired at the licensed body shop of their choice. The same law requires the insurance company to let you know about that right when you first contact them about the damage, and it says an insurer can't require you to use one licensed shop over another.
In plain terms: it's your car, and you get to decide who fixes it.
Why insurance companies recommend shops

Many insurers have "preferred" or "direct repair" shops they work with regularly. Those relationships can make paperwork faster for the insurance company. That doesn't automatically mean a recommended shop is a bad choice, but it does mean you should feel free to compare and pick the shop you trust most.
What to look for in a body shop
When you're deciding where to take your car, consider:
Licensing.
Make sure the shop is a licensed Nevada body shop.
Communication.
You want a shop that explains the damage, the repair plan, and the timeline in plain language.
Experience with your type of vehicle.
A daily driver, a classic, a lifted truck, and a UTV all need different know-how.
Warranty.
Ask what kind of guarantee the shop puts behind its work.
Reviews and reputation.
See what other local drivers are saying.
What about the cost?

Choosing your own shop doesn't mean the insurance company has to pay any price. The law doesn't require an insurer to pay more than what your policy says is reasonable for the repair. A good shop will work directly with your adjuster to document the damage and make sure the repair is done correctly. If additional damage is found once your car is taken apart, the shop can submit a supplement to the insurance company.

title: Paintless Dent Repair vs. Traditional Dent Repair: Which Does Your Car Need?
excerpt: Not every dent is fixed the same way. Here's how paintless dent repair compares to traditional dent repair, and how a shop decides which one fits.
seoTitle: Paintless vs. Traditional Dent Repair in Las Vegas
metaDescription: Compare paintless dent repair and traditional dent repair. Learn which method fits door dings, hail damage, and creased panels in Las Vegas.

children.text: Dents happen. A runaway shopping cart, a door ding in a parking lot, a hailstorm that rolls through out of nowhere. When it comes time to fix one, you'll usually hear about two main approaches: paintless dent repair (PDR) and traditional dent repair. Here's how they differ and how to tell which one your car needs.
What is paintless dent repair?

Paintless dent repair is a technique where a technician works the metal back into shape from behind the panel using specialized tools. Because the original paint isn't sanded, filled, or repainted, your factory finish stays intact.
PDR is often a great fit for:
Small to medium dings and dents
Hail damage
Dents where the paint isn't cracked or chipped
Areas the technician can reach from behind the panel
What is traditional dent repair?

Traditional dent repair is the approach most people picture when they think of body work. The damaged area is reshaped, smoothed with body filler if needed, primed, and then repainted and blended to match the rest of the car.
Traditional repair is usually the right call when:
The paint is cracked, chipped, or scraped
The dent has a sharp crease or stretched metal
The damage is on an edge or body line that PDR can't fully restore
A panel is damaged badly enough that it needs replacing
Which one is better?

Neither method is "better" across the board. It depends on the damage. When PDR is an option, it can save time and keep your original paint, which some owners care a lot about. When the paint is damaged or the metal is stretched, traditional repair is the way to get a finish that looks right and holds up.
How we decide

At The Rebels Garage, we start by looking at the dent in good light, checking the paint, and seeing whether we can access the back of the panel. Then we explain what we see and recommend the approach that gives you the best result. If both options could work, we'll walk you through the differences so you can decide.
Don't wait too long

Even a small dent can turn into a bigger problem if the paint is damaged, since exposed metal can start to corrode over time. If you've got a dent you've been meaning to deal with, it's worth getting it looked at sooner rather than later.

title: How Long Does a Custom Paint Job Take, and What Affects the Cost?
excerpt: A quality custom paint job takes more than a few coats of color. Here's what goes into the process and what drives the timeline and price.
seoTitle: How Long Does a Custom Paint Job Take? | Las Vegas
metaDescription: Thinking about custom paint in Las Vegas? Learn what affects the timeline and cost of a quality paint job, from prep work to color choice.

children.text: A custom paint job can completely change the look of a car. Whether you're bringing a classic back to life, changing colors on a daily driver, or going bold with something eye-catching, one of the first questions people ask is: how long will it take, and what will it cost?
The honest answer is that it depends. Here's what actually drives both.
Prep work is most of the job
The color coat is the part everyone sees, but the quality of a paint job comes from what happens before the paint ever goes on. Prep usually includes:
Removing trim, lights, handles, and other parts
Repairing dents, rust, and imperfections
Sanding the existing finish
Applying primer and blocking it smooth
Skipping or rushing prep is how you end up with peeling, orange peel texture, or flaws showing through the new paint. It's also the biggest reason two paint quotes can look very different.
What affects the timeline
Several things change how long a paint job takes:
Condition of the body.
A car with rust, dents, or old body filler needs more work before painting.
Scope.
A single panel, a full respray of the outside, or a complete color change including door jambs and the engine bay are very different jobs.
Color and finish.
Tri-coats, pearls, metallics, candies, and custom finishes often take more steps and more care than a standard solid color.
Curing and finishing.
After paint and clear coat go on, the finish needs time to cure before it's wet sanded and polished for that deep, glassy look.
What affects the cost

The same factors that affect time also affect cost, plus the materials themselves. Premium paints and specialty finishes cost more, and more labor hours mean a higher price. Be cautious of quotes that seem far lower than others. They often leave out prep work or disassembly, and it shows in the final result.
Get a quote based on your car

The best way to know what your project will take is to have the car looked at in person. At The Rebels Garage, we'll look at the condition of your vehicle, talk through the look you want, and give you a clear estimate.

title: Desert Damage: Common UTV and RZR Body Repairs After a Vegas Ride
excerpt: Southern Nevada's trails are a blast, but they're hard on UTVs. Here are the body repairs we see most on RZRs, Can-Ams, and other side-by-sides.
seoTitle: Common UTV & RZR Body Repairs in Las Vegas
metaDescription: From cracked plastics to bent cages, learn the most common UTV, Can-Am, and RZR body repairs after riding the desert around Las Vegas.

children.text: There's no shortage of places to ride around Las Vegas. Dry lakes, washes, rocky trails, and dunes make Southern Nevada a great place to own a UTV. They also make it a great place to damage one. Here are the repairs we see most often on RZRs, Can-Ams, and other side-by-sides.
Cracked and broken plastics

Fenders, hoods, side panels, and doors take a beating from rocks, brush, and the occasional rollover. Plastic body panels can crack, warp, or snap at mounting points. Depending on the damage, panels can sometimes be repaired, while others are better off replaced.
Bent roll cages

A rollover or a hard hit can bend or damage the cage. The cage is a key safety part of your machine, so any damage should be inspected carefully before you ride again. Don't assume it's fine just because it still looks mostly straight.
Suspension and A-arm damage

Rocks and ledges can bend A-arms, tie rods, and other suspension parts. If your machine pulls to one side, the steering feels off, or a wheel looks like it's sitting at a strange angle, it's time to have it checked.
Bumper, skid plate, and guard damage

Front bumpers, skid plates, and rock sliders do exactly what they're designed to do: take hits so the rest of the machine doesn't. After a while, though, they get bent, cracked, or torn loose from their mounts.
Paint, wraps, and graphics
Desert sand and brush can scratch paint and tear up wraps over time. If your machine has custom paint or graphics, small damage can often be touched up before it spreads.
Why it pays to fix damage early

It's tempting to keep riding with a cracked fender or a loose panel, but small damage tends to get worse on the trail. A loose panel can catch on brush and rip off. A bent suspension part can wear out tires and other components. Getting repairs done between rides keeps your machine safer and saves money in the long run.

title: Signs Your Car's Frame Is Bent After a Collision
excerpt: Frame damage isn't always obvious. Here are the warning signs that your vehicle's frame or unibody may have been damaged in an accident.
seoTitle: Signs Your Car's Frame Is Bent | Las Vegas Frame Repair
metaDescription: Worried about frame damage after a collision? Learn the warning signs of a bent frame or unibody and why a professional inspection matters.

children.text: After an accident, most people focus on the damage they can see: a crumpled bumper, a dented door, a broken headlight. But some of the most important damage is the kind you can't easily spot. If your vehicle's frame or unibody was bent in a collision, it can affect how the car drives, how it wears, and how well it protects you in the future.
Here are the signs to watch for.
Gaps that don't line up

Walk around your car and look at the spaces between panels, like between the hood and fenders or between the doors and the body. If the gaps are uneven from one side to the other, or wider than they used to be, the structure underneath may have shifted.
Doors, hood, or trunk that don't close right
If a door suddenly takes extra force to close, doesn't latch cleanly, or rubs, that's a common clue. The same goes for a hood or trunk lid that won't sit flush.
The car pulls or the steering wheel is off center

A vehicle that drifts to one side or a steering wheel that sits crooked when you're driving straight can point to alignment problems. Sometimes it's just an alignment issue, but after a collision it can also be a sign of frame or suspension damage.
Uneven tire wear
If one tire starts wearing faster than the others, or wears unevenly across the tread, something may be out of alignment underneath the car.
Strange noises
Creaks, squeaks, or clunks that weren't there before the accident can come from parts of the body or suspension that are no longer sitting where they should.
Visible damage underneath

Kinks, bends, cracks, or rust in the frame rails or underbody are clear warning signs. You may not be able to see these without the car on a lift, which is one reason a professional inspection is so important.
Why frame damage needs to be fixed right

Your vehicle's structure is designed to absorb and redirect energy in a crash. If it's bent, it may not do that job the way it was designed to. Proper frame straightening uses measuring equipment to compare the vehicle to factory specifications and bring it back into position.
Get it checked
If you've been in an accident and notice any of these signs, have your vehicle inspected. At The Rebels Garage, we can check for structural damage and explain exactly what we find.

title: RV and Box Truck Body Damage: Why Bigger Vehicles Need a Specialized Shop
excerpt: RVs and box trucks aren't just big cars. Here's why repairing them takes the right space, materials, and experience.
seoTitle: RV & Box Truck Body Repair in Las Vegas
metaDescription: Need RV or box truck body repair in Las Vegas? Learn why larger vehicles need a shop with the space, materials, and experience to fix them right.

children.text: When an RV or box truck gets damaged, a lot of owners run into the same problem: many body shops simply aren't set up to work on them. Larger vehicles come with their own challenges, and getting them repaired right takes a shop that knows how to handle them.
Size matters

The most obvious challenge is space. RVs and box trucks need room to maneuver, room to work around, and room to sit while repairs are completed. Not every shop has bays or lot space that can accommodate them.
Different materials and construction

Bigger vehicles are often built differently than passenger cars. Many RVs use fiberglass or aluminum siding, and box trucks often have aluminum or composite box panels mounted on a separate chassis. Repairing these materials takes different techniques than repairing the steel or aluminum panels on a typical car.
Common types of damage
Some of the repairs we see most often include:
Low clearance strikes on the roof or upper corners
Side swipes from tight turns, gas stations, or parking lots
Damaged rear bumpers, doors, and lift gates
Cracked fiberglass and damaged siding
Paint damage and fading from the Las Vegas sun
Downtime costs money

For businesses that rely on box trucks, every day a truck is off the road affects deliveries and revenue. For RV owners, damage can mean missing out on a planned trip. That's why clear communication and a realistic timeline matter just as much as the repair itself.
Water damage is a real risk

On RVs especially, damage to the roof, seams, or siding can let water in. Even in the desert, a small opening can lead to bigger problems inside the walls over time. If your RV took a hit, it's a good idea to have it inspected even if the damage looks small.
